requested.title: Unauthenticated /mcp get_section accepts an unbounded sections array and fans out with no dedupe — memory/IO amplification DoS
MCP HttpTransport mounted with default in-memory session managers on a public route: every initialize permanently retains attacker data
Attacker-controlled slug interpolated into log lines without sanitization or length clamp
The drift guard aggregates matches across both globals, so a regression in __mochi_page_entry is silent
Protocol-relative URLs (//evil.com) are misclassified as internal and skip rel hardening
An unknown author slug in one post's frontmatter makes /feed.xml 500 on every request

parsedVerdicts.reasoning:
Verified every link in the chain. (1) The schema at mcp.ts:50-52 is `v.object({ sections: v.array(v.object({ type: v.picklist([...]), slug: v.string() })) })` — no `maxLength` on the array, no length/charset constraint on the slug. (2) tmcp's `tools/call` handler (node_modules/tmcp/src/index.js:483-500) validates *only* against the declared schema via `tool.schema['~standard'].validate(args)` and then calls `execute(validated_args)`; `JSONRPCRequestSchema`'s params is a `looseObject`, so the arguments survive intact, and there is no initialization gate — a single POST with `method: 'tools/call'` reaches the handler without ever calling `initialize`. (3) No rate limit: `/mcp` and `/mcp/` are `Mochi.api(({request}) => respondMcp(request))` with no options (routes.ts:137, 347-348), and the site's `Mochi.serve()` (index.ts:163-251) sets no global `rateLimit`, so `buildLimiter` (Mochi.ts:801-828) hits `if (!options.rateLimit) return null`. The `protection` PoW gate only matches `/demos/protection*`, so it does not cover `/mcp`, and no `maxRequestBodySize` is configured anywhere (Bun's 128 MB default applies). (4) The fan-out is real: `Promise.all(sections.map(...))` starts every element's async callback synchronously, and `getDemoLlmsTxt` (docs.ts:201-210) checks `cache.demoLlmsTxt.has(slug)` synchronously *before* its first await, so N requests for the same slug all miss and all run `buildDemoLlmsTxt` in full — `existsSync` plus `Bun.file().text()` for every entry in that demo's `files.ts`. Even the cheap `doc` path amplifies, because `getDocLlmsTxt` returns `doc.raw.trimEnd() + '
'`, allocating a fresh multi-KB string per entry. (5) The response is materialised three times over: `parts.join('

')`, then `v.parse(CallToolResultSchema, ...)`, then `JSON.stringify(response)` plus `TextEncoder().encode()` in the transport's `#handle_post`. A single ~1-4 MB POST of one repeated valid demo slug therefore yields tens of thousands of concurrent file-read fan-outs (preceded by a synchronous `existsSync` storm that stalls the loop) and a multi-hundred-MB-to-GB response — unauthenticated, unmetered, repeatable. Note an upstream proxy's default `client_max_body_size` (1 MB for stock nginx) would shrink but not remove the amplification (~30k entries still fits), and no proxy config is in this repo to confirm a cap. MEDIUM is appropriate: availability-only, single-site impact.

Confirmed against the installed library source, and it is a genuinely distinct defect from F1 (different line, different mechanism, survives any fix to the `sections` bound). mcp.ts:89 passes only `{ path: null, disableSse: true }`, and HttpTransport's constructor destructuring (node_modules/@tmcp/transport-http/src/index.js:90-105) therefore defaults `sessionManager` to `{ streams: new InMemoryStreamSessionManager(), info: new InMemoryInfoSessionManager() }`. In `InMemoryInfoSessionManager` (node_modules/@tmcp/session-manager/src/index.js) `#client_info` and `#client_capabilities` are plain `Map`s with no cap, no TTL and no sweep; the only removal path is `delete(id)`, reached solely from the transport's `#handle_delete` on an explicit HTTP DELETE naming that exact session id. The session id is `request.headers.get('mcp-session-id') || getSessionId()`, i.e. attacker-supplied or a fresh `crypto.randomUUID()` per request (transport respond(), L554-556), and the transport's own `initialize` listener (L127-138) unconditionally calls `setClientCapabilities(sessionId, capabilities)` and `setClientInfo(sessionId, clientInfo)`. The stored content is attacker-chosen and unbounded: `ClientCapabilitiesSchema` is a valibot **`looseObject`** (validation/index.js:242), so arbitrary extra keys and megabyte-long values are preserved verbatim into the map, and `ImplementationSchema`'s `name`/`version`/`title`/`websiteUrl` are bare `v.string()` with no length limit. Combined with the absence of any rate limit on `/mcp` (verified as in F1) and no configured `maxRequestBodySize`, a scripted loop of `initialize` POSTs grows the heap monotonically for the process lifetime. Two small inaccuracies that do not change the verdict: `#log_level` is not reachable (`#init_logging` returns early because the server declares only `capabilities: { tools: { listChanged: false } }`, so `logging/setLevel` is never registered), and `#subscriptions` needs a resources capability that is likewise absent — so two of the four named maps leak, not four. The attacker must also supply a well-formed `protocolVersion`, which is trivial.

The core claim is correct but only one of the two cited lines is actually injectable, and I want that on record. L78 — `logger.warn(`[mcp] get_section not found: ${missing.join(', ')}`)` — interpolates the *raw, unvalidated* request slug: `missing` is populated whenever `content === null`, i.e. precisely for slugs that matched nothing, so the value is fully attacker-controlled. `slug` is `v.string()` with no charset or length constraint, JSON string literals can carry `\n` and `\u001b`, and `logger.warn` (packages/mochi/src/utils/log.ts:44-49) does `console.warn(yellow('[mochi]'), ...args)` with no neutralisation of control characters — so a slug containing CR/LF (optionally with the dim-ANSI `[mochi]` prefix reproduced) writes attacker-authored lines into the same stdout stream that `consoleLogger` and `handleError` (index.ts:47-58) write to. The site sets `logger: { level: 'log' }` unconditionally, and the deployed image runs `bun run dev:site`, so both log calls are live in production. One request is enough; textbook CWE-117, plus ANSI-escape injection against any operator tailing the logs. L75, however, is **not** injectable: `found` only contains ids whose content resolved non-null, and every resolver requires an exact match against a known slug (`getDoc` → `cache.bySlug.get`, `getPost` → `cache.bySlug.get`, `getDemoLlmsTxt` → `internalDemos().find(d => d.slug === slug)`, or the literal `changelog`), so those slugs are server-side values, not request values. `type` is a picklist and is never injectable on either line. Keeping MEDIUM because the impact is log integrity/forgery rather than confidentiality or privilege — it would arguably be LOW on a finer scale, but MEDIUM is the floor here.

The logic defect is exactly as described. `DEBUG_GLOBALS` holds two names; `matched` is a single counter incremented inside each (non-global) `replace` callback, so a healthy page with both globals present yields 2, and the only consumer — index.ts:106, `if (matched === 0 && html.includes('__mochi_debug'))` — can therefore never distinguish 'both matched' from 'one matched, one drifted'. The precondition compounds it by hard-coding the *other* global's name, so the page-entry case is undetectable even in principle. I confirmed both emission sites and that the regex is coupled to them: Mochi.ts:356 emits `<script>window.__mochi_debug=…</script>` and Mochi.ts:357 emits `<script>window.__mochi_page_entry=…</script>`, whose value is `opts.pageEntry` — an absolute source path, i.e. exactly the slash-shaped string this module exists to make opaque. The existing guard test only asserts `matched >= 1` against real framework output and only asserts `window.__mochi_debug=` is present (debugBarEncode.test.ts:72-76), so nothing covers the page-entry coupling — the finding's recommendation to add per-global reporting plus a one-matches-one-doesn't test is sound. One mitigation the finding misses, which I'm recording because it bounds today's impact: Mochi.ts:357 gates `pageEntryScript` on `liveReloadClientJs`, and the deployed image sets `ENV MOCHI_LIVE_RELOAD=false` (Dockerfile:61), which index.ts:166 turns into `liveReload: false` — so `__mochi_page_entry` is not emitted in the current production deployment at all, and the guard happens to work for the one global that is. The hole becomes live the moment that env var changes (the code path fully supports live reload in dev mode), and the structural claim — the guard cannot detect a per-global regression, contrary to its own docstring — is unambiguously true. BUG severity is right.

The misclassification is real and I traced it precisely. `isInternalLink('//evil.com/x')` returns true at line 12 because the string starts with `/`, so `processLink` returns at line 34 and the node gets neither `target="_blank"` nor `rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow"`, even though the browser resolves `//evil.com/x` against the page scheme and navigates cross-origin. The surrounding tests confirm the intent: there is a 'skips absolute path links' case for `/docs/intro` but no protocol-relative case anywhere in rehypeExternalLinks.test.ts, so this is an unhandled form rather than a deliberate choice. The finding's impact analysis is honest and I verified its two supporting claims: no `Referrer-Policy` header is set anywhere in packages/site or packages/mochi (so the leak is capped by the browser default `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`), and the plugin genuinely feeds both pipelines — the build-time docs/blog compile (index.ts:122) and the runtime `renderMarkdown` used for the GitHub-fetched changelog (lib/markdown.ts:62, lib/changelog.ts:46). With no `target` set there is no `window.opener` handle, so the concrete losses are the missing `nofollow` on an outbound first-party-docs link and the pipeline inconsistency, which is why BUG rather than a security severity is correct. The input is first-party (maintainer-authored markdown, plus the project's own release-please changelog), and I found no protocol-relative links in packages/docs or packages/site/src/blog today — so this is a latent correctness gap in a hardening helper, not a live exploit. The side observation about the catch-all `return true` on parse failure and unknown schemes (lines 17-24) is also accurate as read.

Every step checks out. feed.ts:42 calls `getAuthor(post.author).name` inside the `posts.map`, and authors.ts:15-20 throws `Unknown author slug: …` for anything outside the single-entry `authors` record. blog.ts:78-80 validates only `if (!metadata.author)` — presence, never resolvability — so a typo or a newly-added author passes load-time validation and only detonates later. The permanence claim is right and is the sharpest part of the finding: `cachedFeedXml` is assigned at L47, *after* the whole `posts.map` at L33-45 completes, so the throw escapes with nothing memoised and every subsequent request repeats it; `/feed.xml` is a `Mochi.api()` route, and a non-`MochiHttpError` throw becomes a hard 500 via `routeErrorResponse` (runtime/errors.ts:119-122). The secondary nit is also correct: `DATE_RE = /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/` accepts `2024-13-45`, which `new Date(...).toUTCString()` renders as the literal string `Invalid Date` inside `<pubDate>`. Two refinements. First, the blast radius is slightly wider than stated: BlogPost.svelte:31 also calls `getAuthor(author)` in a `$derived`, so that post's own page 500s too — only `/blog/` (which never resolves authors), the sitemap and the llms.txt routes keep working, so it is a bit less silent than described. Second, a mitigation the finding omits: feed.test.ts exercises `buildFeedXml()` against the real `src/blog` contents and asserts `dc:creator`, so a bad author slug in a published post fails `bun run checks` before it could ship. That is a process guard rather than a code guard, and it does not cover the underlying design issue — validation sitting in the wrong place and a cache that cannot degrade gracefully — so the BUG-severity finding stands.
